name: Listener crossword No 29: Virgil Bi-Millenary Crossword

clue.text: Tros Anchisiade

blocks.note: surface reading: 'Trojan son of Anchises', a bare form of address
setter's reading: the Sibyl's greeting to Aeneas in Aeneid 6 pairs this with a further vocative phrase praising his divine descent

explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes half of a greeting from Aeneid 6.125-6, and the answer is the words that stand beside it in the line.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases address Aeneas: his father Anchises was Trojan and his mother Venus a goddess, so he is offspring of heavenly stock.

clue.text: Hoc omnis turba ad —— effusa ruebat (reversed)

definitions.text: Hoc omnis turba ad —— effusa ruebat

indicators.note: the setter's bracketed instruction to write the missing Latin word backwards in the grid

blocks.clueFragment: Hoc omnis turba ad —— effusa ruebat
blocks.note: Aeneid 6.305: the whole crowd of dead souls rushed pouring out to the riverbanks of the Styx

explanation.surface: The throng of ghosts streaming down to the underworld river, waiting for Charon's ferry.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap takes an accusative plural after 'ad', RIPAS, 'to the banks'; Virgil wrote 'huc' where the clue has 'hoc'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripa is Latin for a riverbank, and the souls crowd onto the banks of the Styx begging to be ferried across.

clue.text: A meaningless palindrome, suggesting the name Titus Optimus

definitions.text: A meaningless palindrome, suggesting the name Titus Optimus

blocks.note: surface reading: a nonsense string that reads the same both ways
setter's reading: initials and an abbreviation for a Roman name, mirrored about a central letter

explanation.surface: A bit of nonsense that happens to hint at an imaginary Roman.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a filler light: T is the standard abbreviation of the praenomen Titus, and the string is built symmetrically round O for Optimus.
explanation.definitionFit: The setter admits the letters mean nothing; they only read identically forwards and backwards while recalling Roman initials.

clue.text: At rabidae tigres absunt et saeva leonum semina, nec miseros fallunt —— legentes (first three letters only)

definitions.text: At rabidae tigres absunt et saeva leonum semina, nec miseros fallunt —— legentes

blocks.clueFragment: At rabidae tigres absunt et saeva leonum semina, nec miseros fallunt —— legentes
blocks.note: Georgics 2.152: in Italy no poisonous plant tricks the unlucky people who gather herbs

explanation.surface: Virgil's praise of Italy: no raging tigers, no lions, and no deadly weeds to deceive the herb-gatherer.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word is ACONITA, the poisonous plants, of which only ACO is entered.
explanation.definitionFit: Aconite, or wolfsbane, is a famously toxic plant easily mistaken for harmless herbs, so it deceives those picking it.

clue.text: Let him take (one letter missing)

indicators.note: a letter is lacking, so the Latin word goes in shortened by one

blocks.note: the Latin third-person present subjunctive of 'capio', used as a command

explanation.surface: An instruction giving someone permission to help himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin for 'let him take' is CAPIAT; its final T is the letter missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin uses the subjunctive for third-person commands, so 'let him take' is the jussive form of the verb to seize.

clue.text: Sole sub ardenti resonant arbusta —— (two letters transposed)

indicators.note: swapping a pair of neighbouring letters is a small rearrangement of the word's order

blocks.note: Georgics 3.328: under the blazing sun the orchards ring with the insects' noise
the gap takes the ablative plural of the Latin name for the singing insect of hot summers

explanation.surface: A hot Italian midday, the trees loud with insect song.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is the ablative plural CICADIS, 'with cicadas'; its A and D swap places in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Cicadas are the insects whose shrill summer chirring fills Mediterranean trees in the heat of the day.

clue.text: —— cum ardente viderent / Scintillare oleum (first three letters only)

indicators.note: keeping only the opening trio means the rest of the word is cut away before entry

blocks.note: Georgics 1.391: girls spinning at night see the oil spit in the burning lamp, a sign of rain

explanation.surface: Women at their evening work watching the lamp oil sputter, a weather sign.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is TESTA, the earthenware lamp, of which only TES is entered.
explanation.definitionFit: Testa is an earthenware vessel, here the clay oil lamp whose burning wick crackles and sparks.

clue.text: —— sic orsa loqui vates

blocks.note: surface reading: the prophetess began to speak thus, with the opening word blank
setter's reading: Aeneid 6.125, where the line opens with the conjunction 'when'

explanation.surface: The Sibyl of Cumae about to deliver her answer to Aeneas.
explanation.walkthrough: The same passage supplies 1 and 30 across: the Sibyl's speech that follows begins 'sate sanguine divum'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin conjunction meaning 'when' introduces the clause in which the prophetess starts speaking.

clue.text: Clamorque virum stridorque ——

blocks.note: surface reading: the shouting of men and a shrieking of something, with the source left blank
setter's reading: Aeneid 1.87, the storm at sea, where the shriek comes from a ship's lines straining in the wind

explanation.surface: Aeneas's fleet caught in Aeolus's storm, sailors yelling over the screaming rigging.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap needs a genitive plural to match 'virum', the shrieking 'of the ropes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudens is Latin for a ship's rope or cable, and taut rigging howls in a gale.

clue.text: MEAE

definitions.note: no real definition: the setter prints the entry itself in place of a clue

clue.text: Two words describing Amyntas (the last six letters somewhat transposed)

indicators.note: partly moved about, so those letters go in out of their normal order

blocks.note: Eclogue 3.66: the shepherd Menalcas calls the boy Amyntas 'my flame', meaning his beloved

explanation.surface: A note on how a shepherd boy is described in the Eclogues.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is IGNIS MEUS; its first three letters stay put and the last six are jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignis meus, 'my fire', is a Latin love endearment, and Menalcas uses it of Amyntas, the boy he loves.

clue.text: Apparet Camerina procul campique —— (reversed)

indicators.note: the setter's bracketed instruction to write the missing Latin word backwards in the grid

blocks.note: Aeneid 3.701: sailing round Sicily, the Trojans see Camerina and the plains of a nearby river

explanation.surface: Sicilian landmarks sliding past as Aeneas's fleet coasts the island.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is GELOI, 'of Gela', the genitive of the river and town on Sicily's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The Geloan plains lie beside the River Gela near Camerina, the next sight on the Trojans' voyage along the coast.

clue.text: Tells of Virgil’s birth (2½ words)

indicators.note: only half of the final word is wanted, so its ending is cut off

blocks.note: the opening of the poet's traditional epitaph at Naples, naming his birthplace

explanation.surface: A note on where the poet was born.
explanation.walkthrough: The epitaph runs 'Mantua me genuit, Calabri rapuere', 'Mantua bore me, Calabria snatched me away'; only the first half of 'genuit' is entered.
explanation.definitionFit: The epitaph's first words record that his home city gave the poet life, so they literally tell of his birth.

clue.text: Facilis descensus —— (reversed and last letter omitted)

indicators.note: leaving out the final character trims the word at its tail before entry
the setter's bracketed instruction to write the remaining letters backwards in the grid

blocks.note: Aeneid 6.126: the descent to the underworld is easy

explanation.surface: The Sibyl's famous warning that going down to the dead is easy and coming back is hard.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is AVERNO; Avernus is the crater lake near Cumae thought to be the entrance to the underworld. Drop the final O and turn the rest round.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says the way down to the lake at the gate of the dead is easy, so the gap names that destination.

clue.text: Et ventis et fulminis —— alis (first three letters only)

indicators.note: keeping only the opening trio means the rest of the word is cut away before entry

blocks.note: Aeneid 5.319: in the footrace Nisus shoots ahead, quicker than the winds and the lightning's wings

explanation.surface: A runner bursting away from the field at the funeral games.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is the comparative OCIOR, 'swifter', of which only OCI is entered.
explanation.definitionFit: Ocior means faster, and the line compares the sprinter's speed with wind and winged lightning.

clue.text: Tyrrhenusque tubae —— per aethera clangor (first three letters only)

indicators.note: keeping only the opening trio means the rest of the word is cut away before entry

blocks.note: Aeneid 8.526: an Etruscan trumpet blast seems to bellow across the sky as an omen

explanation.surface: A heavenly omen: the blare of a war trumpet roaring through the air.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is the infinitive MUGIRE, 'to bellow', of which only MUG is entered.
explanation.definitionFit: Mugire is the Latin verb for the lowing of cattle, used here of the deep roar of the trumpet.

clue.text: An imaginary proverb (two words) analogous to “pearls before swine”

definitions.text: An imaginary proverb (two words) analogous to “pearls before swine”

blocks.note: surface reading: a made-up Latin saying the solver is asked to invent
setter's reading: a gift wasted on a creature that cannot appreciate it, phrased as a dative recipient and the sweet thing given

explanation.surface: A request for a Latin equivalent of the biblical warning against wasting good things.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words mean 'honey to a whale': cetus is a whale or sea monster, in the dative, and mel is honey.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving a sweet delicacy to a vast sea beast is as pointless as casting precious jewels to hogs.

clue.text: Tum se ad Cairtae —— fert litore portum (vowels omitted)

definitions.text: Tum se ad Cairtae —— fert litore portum

indicators.note: dropping every vowel leaves only the consonant skeleton of the word

blocks.clueFragment: Tum se ad Cairtae —— fert litore portum
blocks.note: Aeneid 6.900: Aeneas sails straight along the shore to the harbour of Caieta

explanation.surface: Aeneas leaving the underworld and making directly for port along the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is RECTO, 'straight'; the clue's 'Cairtae' is a misprint for Caietae, and Virgil has 'limite' for 'litore'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rectus means straight, so the ship runs on a direct course to Caieta's harbour.

clue.text: Two thirds (letters transposed)

indicators.note: the letters swap positions, so the word goes in rearranged

blocks.note: the Latin noun for two-thirds of a whole, originally eight twelfths of an as

explanation.surface: A plain fraction.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin word is BES; Roman fractions were counted in twelfths (unciae) of the as, and eight twelfths make two thirds.
explanation.definitionFit: Bes was the Roman unit for eight unciae, which is exactly two parts in three of a whole.

clue.text: Anag. of neuter plural of the adjective of a town built on the site of the ancient Sybaris

definitions.text: neuter plural of the adjective of a town built on the site of the ancient Sybaris

blocks.clueFragment: neuter plural of the adjective of a town built on the site of the ancient Sybaris
blocks.note: the Greek colony of Thurii was founded close to ruined Sybaris in southern Italy

explanation.surface: A grammar question about a town in the heel of Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The town is Thurii, its adjective Thurinus, and the neuter plural THURINA is entered jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin adjectives end in -a in the neuter plural, so the form agreeing with neuter plural nouns is Thurina.

clue.text: Long

blocks.note: surface reading: the English adjective for great length
setter's reading: the adverb 'for a long time', to be put into Latin

explanation.walkthrough: As throughout this puzzle, the English is to be rendered in Latin, and 'long' is read as the adverb of time, not of size.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin adverb diu means for a lengthy while, as in 'he waited long'.

explanation.walkthrough: The gap is OPIS, genitive of 'ops', 'power'; its I is the vowel left out.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Non opis est nostrae' means 'it is not in our power', ops being resources or ability.

explanation.definitionFit: Cubitum is Latin for the elbow, which Dido leans on as she tries to lift herself.

clue.text: Generally means a trumpet in Virgil

definitions.text: Generally means a trumpet in Virgil

blocks.note: surface reading: a word whose ordinary sense is something else
setter's reading: the metal of which trumpets were made, which the poet uses for the instrument itself

explanation.walkthrough: Virgil often names the trumpet by its material, as in 'aere ciere viros', 'to rouse men with the bronze'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin for bronze or copper stands for a brass instrument by metonymy, naming a thing by its substance.

clue.text: In which direction (one letter omitted)

indicators.note: a single letter is dropped, so the word goes in one short

blocks.note: the Latin adverb asking which of two ways

explanation.surface: A traveller's question about which way to go.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin word is UTRO, 'in which of two directions'; its R is the letter left out.
explanation.definitionFit: Utro is the adverb of 'uter', which of two, so it asks towards which side something moves.

clue.text: Saxa ciet, scatebrisque —— temperat arva (first five letters)

indicators.note: only the opening five are kept, so the tail of the word is cut away

blocks.note: Georgics 1.110: irrigation water tumbles over stones and with its gushing cools the parched fields

explanation.surface: A farmer channelling a stream to refresh his thirsty fields.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is ARENTIA, 'dry', agreeing with 'arva'; only ARENT goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Arens means parched, from 'areo', to be dry, describing the sun-baked fields the water revives.

clue.text: Bellantum litousque pati —— que —— ferre —— et stabulo frenos audire sonantes (last two letters omitted)

blocks.note: Georgics 3.183-5: training a young horse to bear trumpets, a creaking wheel being dragged, and jingling bridles in the stall

explanation.surface: Advice on getting a colt used to the sounds of war and harness.
explanation.walkthrough: The words are 'tractu(que) gementem ferre rotam', 'to bear the wheel groaning as it is dragged'; the attached 'que' is printed, and ROTAM loses AM. 'Litousque' is a misprint for 'lituosque'.

clue.text: Lucentemque globum junae Titaniaque astra ——, totamque infusa per artus mens agitat molem et magno se corpore miscet

definitions.text: Lucentemque globum junae Titaniaque astra ——, totamque infusa per artus mens agitat molem et magno se corpore miscet

blocks.note: surface reading: Aeneid 6.725-7, Anchises explaining what sustains the moon and stars
setter's reading: the gap is the clause naming an inner breath that nourishes the whole universe, which mind then moves

explanation.surface: Anchises in the underworld expounding the world-soul that animates all creation.
explanation.walkthrough: Virgil wrote 'spiritus intus alit', 'a spirit within nourishes'; the grid splits it, with 60 holding the first and last words and 27 down the middle one. 'Junae' is a misprint for 'lunae'.
explanation.definitionFit: The passage is Stoic cosmology: an indwelling breath feeds sky, sea, moon and stars, and mind stirs the mass.

clue.text: —— natorum sanguine matrem commaculare manus

explanation.definitionFit: Saevus means savage and docuit means taught, so the words make passion the instructor of the crime.

clue.text: Ambo florentes aetatibus —— (last letter omitted)

explanation.definitionFit: Arcadia in the Peloponnese was the ideal home of shepherd-singers, so both herdsmen are described as natives of it.

clue.text: —— —— surdis, respondent omnia silvae

explanation.walkthrough: The full line is 'we do not sing to the deaf: the woods answer everything'.

clue.text: ‘A loftier Argo cleaves the main / Fraught with a later prize’. (Three words of the Virgilian quotation)

definitions.text: ‘A loftier Argo cleaves the main / Fraught with a later prize’

blocks.clueFragment: ‘A loftier Argo cleaves the main / Fraught with a later prize’
blocks.note: surface reading: Shelley's chorus from Hellas, about a new golden age

blocks.clueFragment: Three words of the Virgilian quotation
blocks.note: setter's reading: Shelley echoes Eclogue 4.34-5, and the wanted words come from Virgil's line about a second Argo carrying heroes
